## URBAN RIGHT TO SHADE ORDINANCE (DRETUMB)

Image

[ORIGINAL EN CATALÀ] [TRADUCCIÓN AL ESPAÑOL]

#### PROTOCOL: DISPUTATIONS IN THE SHADE

In our itinerant spatial activations, the Department of Umbrology aims to establish protective shades to map, describe, and contest territorial grievances (demographic shifts; thermal comfort, accessibility, and the right to green spaces; housing conditions; opacity and surveillance, etc.) through ephemeral interventions intended for public visibility, awareness, and the socio-ecological protection of contested sites.

We seek to temporarily occupy these shaded areas not only as sites of fleeting protection, but as true urban parliaments: nomadic architectures designed to accommodate diverse living beings and their respective concerns; spaces to deliberate upon our right to shade, driving toward climate sovereignty and grassroots self-protection protocols.

Consequently, we call for the shading of public spaces to serve as democratic platforms, where shadows accommodate a plurality of urban definitions for the city’s various living beings: that is, as spaces for multispecies relations intended to suspend the solar order of traditional urban planning. We designate these activities as disputations in the shade.

It is our intent that these disputations—drawing inspiration from the Parlement de Loire and its continuation in the internationale des rivières et autres éléments de la nature, or the Court for Intergenerational Climate Crimes—act as vehicles for a popular inventive statecraft or, in other words, serve the public imagination in responding to the urban challenges of the ongoing climatic mutation.

In these disputations in the shade, we would like to create a space for listening to umbrological grievances —fostering the expression of the problems of solar urbanism experienced by a diversity of bodies— and, in response, open for public comment the following draft of an Urban Right to Shade Ordinance (DRETUMB), conceived as an instrument to reclaim our right as holobionts to devise new forms of self-protection, transcending the solar regime of currently instituted urbanism.

We welcome all submissions to dispute, enrich, expand, specify, amend, and adopt this text as your own!

#### PUBLIC CALL FOR COMMENT: URBAN RIGHT TO SHADE ORDINANCE (DRETUMB)

(Version 1.0, Summer 2026 – This is a true and accurate translation of the original ordinance drafted in Catalan. For all legal purposes, the Catalan original text shall be consulted as the sole authentic and official version)


Shade is hereby defined as a dynamic common good: a nomadic atmospheric flow resulting from the interception of solar radiation, constituting the minimal and essential infrastructure required to maintain the city within a habitable thermal threshold.

Inspired by the Habitability Principle outlined by Baptiste Morizot and Laurent Neyret, the theses on Ecological Redirection by the Origens Medialab, the explorations of political biotic communities within the Zoöp Model, and the urban climate policy guidelines Decoding Comfort, the Department of Umbrology hereby proclaims the seasonal right to urban shade and vindicates penumbra and opacity (as conceptualized by Édouard Glissant) as a climate shelter for holobionts. Accordingly, pursuant to its Guide: The City of Shades, urban shade is established as a fundamental protection for all living bodies, ensuring they are not left fully exposed and vulnerable to solar irradiation.
##### TITLE IV: CLIMATE SELF-PROTECTION AND TEMPORARY OCCUPATION OF SPACE

Shaded areas shall be respected as shelters for shared rest and penumbra. All municipal or commercial activities that disrupt such refuge are suspended.

# The Inoperative Refusal: Gestures and How the Unruly Body Goes on Strike

Thuỳ-Trang T. Nguyen,

## ABSTRACT

This paper advances a way of thinking the body in human geography through gestures, their capacity to refuse inoperatively and their relation to unconscious processes. Extending insights from non-representational and embodied approaches to gestures in the field, it treats gestures as a distinct analytic and develops the concept of ‘inoperative refusal’ to account for how unconscious, corporeal practices interrupt axes of bodily discipline and surveillance without becoming intentional or representational forms of resistance. Through gestures, the body refuses. Drawing on a psychoanalytic reading of gestures via the work of Donald Winnicott, the paper reclaims the unconscious for the body and situates queer gestures as instances of the inoperative refusal. To examine how such refusal might operate collectively, I place it in dialogue with Herbert Marcuse's ‘Great Refusal’ (1955) and Maurice Blanchot's ‘pure means’ refusal (2010), which offer resources for thinking refusal towards non-programmatic forms of collective action. Moving beyond intentionality and negativity, I suggest that the inoperative refusal resides in ambiguity and indeterminacy, not the oppositional. The inoperative refusal affirms the open-endedness of the horizon of becoming while inviting a rethinking of solidarity as that which already takes place in the everyday attunement of bodies in gestures, where feelings of kinship and shared worlding may unexpectedly arise and exceed political identification.

## 1 Introduction

In the hallucinatory verses of Notebook of a Return to the Native Land, Aime Césaire laments: ‘I have assassinated God with my laziness with my words with my gestures with my obscene songs’ (2001, 19). At the same time, there remains some ambiguity regarding the degree to which refusal may be understood as a conscious and strategic decision. Accounts grounded in Indigenous politics often emphasise refusal as an intentional act: a deliberate withholding, disengagement or non-compliance that asserts sovereignty and sets limits on recognition. Recent work in human geography suggests a different but complementary approach. Analyses of encounters within politically constrained environments indicate that what is interpreted as refusal can emerge through situated, relational and sometimes tacit practices. Jones (2012) follows the unauthorised border-crossing into India by a 62-year-old woman from Bangladesh, where she works as a servant for a wealthy family, to spend a month visiting her son and grandson. Jones's concept of ‘spaces of refusal’ shows how everyday practices of evasion and disregard can refuse to abide by the state's binary territorial and identity categories, even when they do not take the form of overt political resistance. Accordingly, refusal may involve partial disengagement, strategic ambiguity or forms of non-participation that are not always framed by participants themselves as deliberate acts. From this perspective, refusal may be better understood as a situated practice that is not reducible to conscious, intentional decision-making, including more ambiguous forms of disengagement under conditions of constraint. Following this thread of ambiguity, recent studies attending to gestures in human geography are concerned with how gestures articulate a certain politics of refusal by Black queer women in American gentrifying neighbourhoods (Adeyemi 2019; Seitz and Proudfoot 2021), by Palestinian people expressing humour and laughter in the heavily surveilled environment of border control security (Bhungalia 2020), and by people in Delhi taking over unfinished urban development projects ‘through practices of squatting and repair’ (Boudreau 2023; Simone et al. 2023).

This paper contributes to this thread of scholarship tracing the ambiguity of refusal through a theorisation of gestures as the medium through which the body goes on strike—unlike a conventional labour strike because it operates without intentionality—or, in other words, its inoperative refusal. To find one of the most sustained engagements with gestures and the connection between the psyche and the body, I will now turn to psychoanalysis and the writing of Winnicott. It is in this literature that I will argue for a reclaiming of the unconscious for the body via gestures.

What is a 'Shadow Report'? 
A Shadow Report is a report to the Committee from a source other 
than the Government. By becoming a party to the Covenant (signature 
in 1968, ratification in 1978), New Zealand voluntarily agreed to 
participate in the Committee's reporting and monitoring process.  
Every few years there is an exchange of reports and correspondence, 
and an interactive dialogue session in Geneva or New York between 
the Committee, and the Government.  
The last examination under the Covenant was concluded in March 
2010,5 following which the Committee released a report with 
recommendations6 (“Concluding Observations”). The Committee’s 
concluding observations (along with its ‘views’ on individual 
communications submitted under the First Optional Protocol to the 
Covenant, and ‘General Comments’ elaborating the understanding of 
specific provisions of the Covenant) while not formally binding as a 
matter of law, constitute authoritative interpretations of international 
human rights law.

In other words, every bride has an inalienable right to the services of her pastor. To violate that right is to bring a shadow into her life when there should be no shadows.

Moreover, when she violates the highest standards of her church, the meaning of consecration, and her own best interests, she forfeits her inalienable right both to her pastor and to a shadowless marriage. Cosenza scaffolds his thesis through a reconstruction of the conceptual “flow” running through Lacan’s sparse, often elliptical remarks on anorexia across the span of his teaching. This effort allows for the articulation of the logic underlying the symptom’s core performative gesture, and for a mapping of the structural coordinates that this refusal responds to. The anorexic’s radical “no” is thus traced through four distinct positions Lacan assumed throughout the evolution of his thought. In the process, what emerges is not only a reading of anorexia but also an implicit masterclass in Lacan’s theoretical development, curated around the traces of a single signifier.

Cosenza takes off with Lacan’s earliest comments in “The Family Complexes” from 1938, where—still under Kleinian influence—the young Lacan conceives of anorexia as a refusal of weaning, a resistance to separating from the maternal rapport. This position, Cosenza notes, Lacan later abandons, only to return to it much later in his teaching, but reframed: not as a clinging to the maternal imago, but as a drive toward unity with the One—the omnipotent, seamless rapport that retains the trace of the maternal, is now articulated through Lacan’s critique of the discourse of the markets and its emblematic rejection of lack. It inscribes the irreducibility of desire in the field of demand. Within the hysterical matrix, the anorexic’s refusal becomes a metonymic substitution for the desire of the Other. Her fantasy of disappearance poses the unbearable question: Does he want to lose me? In the analytic transference, this often emerges as a threat of withdrawal—a temptation to interrupt treatment precisely when symbolic work begins. Refusal, at this level, becomes an unconscious demand for interpretation, asking to be read even as it expels meaning. It is, in this, dimension, Job’s diatribe with God.

From a Lacanian-Millerian perspective, refusal is primarily, the refusal of the Other: “…the rejection of the Other, in particular of the nurturing mother and more broadly the rejection of the great Other” (Miller & Laurent, as cited in Cosenza, 2023, p. 78). This refusal has a double genitive structure stressed by Miller: the Other who refuses the subject, putting the subject in the position of waste through what Recalcati calls the “grimace of the Other” (as cited in Cosenza, 2023, p. 87) that has its effects in the mirror function. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
